1037.title: Rama's promise: do not fear
1037.hook: Ravana's own brother crosses to Rama's camp, and Rama makes a vow the raised palm still keeps
1037.carry: abhaya: the god's promise to anyone who comes
1037.tomorrow: why did Brahma make a fifth Veda?
1037.howItsDone: Devotees meet abhaya and varada mudras on the images of deities in temples and home shrines; the raised open palm is read as "do not fear" and the lowered open palm as the giving of blessings. Many pray before them when they are afraid, and Sri Vaishnava teachers cite Rama's vow to Vibhishana as a great promise of refuge (sharanagati).

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THIRTY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: All week, the mudras have been shapes you make with your own hands. Today, one is held out to you, and it comes with a story.
screen: `THE MUDRAS.` · `A HAND HELD OUT TO YOU.`

segments.voice: Before the war, while Rama's army waits on the shore, a figure comes across the sea to Rama's camp. It's Vibhishana, younger brother of Ravana, the king who stole Sita. He begged his brother to give her back, and was thrown out for it. Now he hangs in the sky above the monkey army and asks for refuge. Below him, Sugriva, the monkey king, says what everyone is thinking. It's a trick. He's Ravana's brother. He's a spy.
screen: `RAVANA'S BROTHER CROSSES OVER.` → `IT'S A TRICK, SAYS SUGRIVA.` → `RAMA'S ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Rama hears out the whole camp. Some say test him first; Hanuman says his face shows no deceit. Then Rama answers, in Valmiki's Ramayana, here in paraphrase: to anyone who comes to me even once and says, I am yours, I give fearlessness from all beings. That is my vow. Bring him in. Even if it were Ravana himself. The word Rama uses for that gift is abhayam: fearlessness. Now stand before a temple image, Shiva dancing, Durga, Rama himself. One hand is raised, open, palm toward you, fingers up. That's abhaya mudra, the gesture of that same gift: do not be afraid. Often a second hand hangs low, palm open, fingers down: varada mudra, the hand that grants what is asked. Here's the teaching. In Hindu devotion, turning to God even once, even from the wrong side of the war, is enough to be taken in. Teachers call that turning sharanagati, taking refuge, and many Vaishnava teachers count Rama's vow among its great promises. So the raised palm isn't decoration, and it isn't stop. It's a promise standing in the room. That's why frightened people, before surgery, before an exam, before a first day, go and stand in front of it. The Gita adds one more layer: in its sixteenth chapter, the list of qualities that lean toward the divine begins with the same word, abhayam. Many teachers read the palm both ways: a promise of protection, and a fearlessness meant to grow in the one who looks.
screen: `EVEN ONCE: I AM YOURS.` · `ABHAYA MUDRA: THE GIFT OF FEARLESSNESS.` · `VARADA: THE HAND THAT GIVES.` · `SHARANAGATI: TAKING REFUGE.` · then, large: `A PROMISE STANDING IN THE ROOM.`

segments.voice: Let the left hand rest beside the left knee, palm open and turned forward, fingers down: the giving hand. Raise the right hand to shoulder height, palm forward, fingers relaxed: do not fear. Breathe slowly, and if a worry comes, let it meet the raised palm without arguing. If you pray, face a home shrine and say silently, I am yours. If not, just rest in the two shapes.
The mudras. Today, two you receive: abhaya, the raised palm that says do not fear, and varada, the low open hand that gives.
screen: `THE MUDRAS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: abhaya, the god's promise to anyone who comes. Tomorrow: why did Brahma make a fifth Veda? Back tomorrow, same hill.

1038.title: The fifth Veda: dance as worship
1038.hook: the gods ask Brahma for something everyone can see and hear, and he makes dance and drama a Veda
1038.carry: natya, the fifth veda: dance offered to god
1038.tomorrow: how can chopping vegetables be worship?
1038.howItsDone: In classical Indian dance forms such as Bharatanatyam and Odissi, dancers begin with a bow to the earth and an offering to the deity, then use named hand gestures (hastas) and facial expression to tell stories, often of the gods; the Natya Shastra tells how Brahma made drama and dance a fifth Veda.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THIRTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mudras you receive: abhaya, the god's promise to anyone who comes, held out in a raised palm. Today the hands start to move, and the story goes back to where dance began.
screen: `THE MUDRAS.` · `ABHAYA: DO NOT FEAR.`

segments.voice: The old manual of drama, the Natya Shastra, opens with sages asking its teacher, Bharata, where all this came from. He tells a story. Long ago the world had slid into greed, anger and trouble, and the gods went to Brahma with a request. The Vedas, they said, are not heard by everyone. Make something else: something to see and to hear, for every kind of person. A fifth Veda.
screen: `THE WORLD SLIDES INTO TROUBLE.` → `THE GODS GO TO BRAHMA.` → `MAKE A FIFTH VEDA.`

segments.voice: Brahma sat in thought and drew from all four. From the Rig Veda he took the words. From the Sama Veda, song. From the Yajur Veda, abhinaya, the art of acting it out. From the Atharva Veda, rasa, the taste of feeling. He called it the Natyaveda and gave it to Bharata, and later in the telling Shiva adds his fierce dance, the tandava, and Parvati her graceful one. Here's the teaching inside the origin story. In Hinduism, dance and drama aren't just entertainment beside religion. They were made as a Veda, a way of knowing, open to anyone who can watch. That's why classical dancers begin by bowing: touching the floor, which many explain as asking the earth's pardon for stamping on her, and offering the dance to the deity. On the stage, the hands do the speaking. A later dancers' manual, the Abhinaya Darpana, lists them one by one: pataka, the flag; mukula, the bud; hamsasya, the swan's beak. One shape can be a cloud, a forest or a blessing, and the story tells you which. It also gives a chain dancers love to quote, in paraphrase: where the hand goes, the eyes follow; where the eyes go, the mind; where the mind goes, the feeling; and where the feeling goes, rasa arises. A hand moving in the lamplight, and a whole room tasting devotion. So when a girl in a New Jersey studio rehearses a poem about Krishna, by her tradition's own story, she's studying a Veda.
screen: `WORDS, SONG, ACTING, FEELING.` · `THE NATYAVEDA: FOR EVERYONE.` · `BOW TO THE EARTH, OFFER THE DANCE.` · `HAND, EYES, MIND, FEELING, RASA.` · then, large: `DANCE IS AN OFFERING.`

segments.voice: Begin the way dancers do: touch the floor lightly with your right hand, then bring it to your eyes. Make pataka, the flag: hand flat, fingers together, thumb bent in, in front of your chest. Move it slowly out to the right and back, then to the left, eyes following the hand. If you pray, let the movement be your offering; if not, just notice whether the mind follows the eyes.
The mudras. In dance, hastas: hand shapes that tell a story, where the hand leads and the eyes, the mind and the feeling follow.
screen: `THE MUDRAS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: natya, the fifth Veda, dance offered to God. Tomorrow: how can chopping vegetables be worship? See you then.

1039.title: Savata the gardener: work as worship
1039.hook: a gardener near Pandharpur sings that his onions, radishes and greens are all his god
1039.carry: svakarma: your own work, offered, is worship
1039.tomorrow: where does Krishna say he can be found?
1039.howItsDone: Many Hindus offer their daily work as worship: a cook offers the first portion before anyone eats, tools are honored at Ayudha Puja, and devotees recall the Gita's teaching (18.46) that one worships God through one's own work, and the Varkari saints who sang it, such as Savata Mali.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THIRTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fifth Veda: dance and drama, made by Brahma for everyone, and offered back to God. Today the last of the mudras, and the hands go to work.
screen: `THE MUDRAS.` · `THE FIFTH VEDA.`

segments.voice: Near Pandharpur, in Maharashtra, the town of the god Vitthala, there lived a gardener named Savata. People still call him Savata Mali, Savata the gardener. Every year crowds of pilgrims walk past fields like his, singing, on their way to the temple. In the stories told about him, Savata stays in his field. Weeding. Watering. Pulling onions. And he sings one of the plainest songs any saint ever sang.
screen: `A GARDENER NEAR PANDHARPUR.` → `HE STAYS IN HIS FIELD.` → `THE PLAINEST SONG.`

segments.voice: Savata belongs to the Varkaris, the singing saints of Maharashtra, in the time of Jnaneshwar and Namdev, some seven hundred years ago. His best-loved line is about vegetables. In paraphrase: onion, radish, greens, all of it is my Vitthala. Not a picture of God beside the vegetables. The vegetables. The stories say that when he wouldn't leave his work for the temple, the god came out to the field instead. The teaching behind the song is as old as the Gita. In its last chapter, Krishna says, in paraphrase: the one from whom all beings come, who pervades all this, worship him with your own work, and you reach perfection. Svakarma: your own work, offered. Earlier, in chapter thirteen, the Gita describes that same reality with an image for this week of hands: its hands and feet are everywhere. And the very next verse adds that it has no senses of its own, and holds up everything while clinging to none. Hands everywhere, and bound to none. So this is the widest mudra. A hand shaped before a shrine means something on purpose. A hand pulling an onion, slicing bread or counting change can mean the same thing, if it's offered. That's why a cook may offer the first portion before anyone eats, why people honor their tools at Ayudha Puja, why a shop may open with a small prayer at the counter. The tradition doesn't say a job is worship by itself. It says your own work, done well and offered, already is.
screen: `ONION, RADISH, GREENS: MY VITTHALA.` · `GITA 18: WORSHIP WITH YOUR OWN WORK.` · `GITA 13: HANDS AND FEET EVERYWHERE.` · `THE WIDEST MUDRA.` · then, large: `YOUR WORK, OFFERED, IS WORSHIP.`

segments.voice: Rest the hands on the thighs, palms up, and look at them: the lines, the knuckles, the places that do the work. Close the eyes and let other hands from your day come and go, the ones that grew and cooked your food, the ones that built your chair. Then think of one task waiting for you today. If you pray, offer it silently before you start: this is for you. If not, decide to do it well, for someone.
The mudras. Today, the widest: hands and feet everywhere, and a gardener's hands that made their work a prayer.
screen: `THE MUDRAS — today's word`.

1040.title: Krishna in the best of everything
1040.hook: Arjuna asks where to look for Krishna, and the answer runs from the ocean to the first letter, a
1040.carry: vibhuti: god shines in the best of everything
1040.tomorrow: how did a robber become a saint by saying a name backwards?
1040.howItsDone: Hindus honor the divine shining in the greatest of each kind, as Krishna lists in Gita 10: bathing in the Ganga, folding hands to the sea, going on pilgrimage to great mountains; students of Sanskrit also learn that the letter a, which Krishna names among letters, sounds inside almost every consonant.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-FORTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last of the mudras: Savata the gardener, and your own work, offered, as worship. Today the hands rest, the mouth begins, and the first sound comes from Krishna himself.
screen: `THE MUDRAS.` · `YOUR WORK, OFFERED.`

segments.voice: In the middle of the Gita, on the battlefield, Arjuna has just heard that his friend and charioteer is the source of everything. So he asks what anyone would ask next. How do I keep you in mind? In what things should I think of you? Tell me again, he says. I never get tired of hearing it.
screen: `YOU ARE THE SOURCE OF EVERYTHING.` → `WHERE DO I LOOK FOR YOU?` → `TELL ME AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Krishna answers with a list, one of the loveliest in the Gita. Among waters, I am the ocean. Among things that stand firm, the Himalaya. Among trees, the sacred fig. Among rivers, the Ganga. And then, in paraphrase: among letters, I am the letter a. Then he gives the key to the whole list: whatever is glorious, beautiful or mighty, know that it springs from a spark of my splendor. And: I hold up this whole world with one small part of myself. These are his vibhutis, his shinings: places where the divine shows through most clearly. Here's the teaching. Krishna doesn't say the ocean is all of God. He says God shines in the best of each kind, so an ocean, a great river or a mountain can lead the mind to him. That's why a family at the beach may fold their hands to the sea, why the Ganga is bathed in as holy, and why pilgrims walk around Mount Kailasa. Now the letter. A is the plainest sound there is: open the mouth, let the voice out, don't shape it. A. It's where the Sanskrit alphabet begins. And in Devanagari, the script Sanskrit is often written in, a consonant carries a short a inside it unless a mark says otherwise. The letter for k is read ka; for m, ma. So the a runs, quietly, through almost every letter on the page. Many teachers read that as Krishna's point: the divine is the plainest thing, running through everything else. This week, the sounds of the sacred words, and what they carry.
screen: `OCEAN, HIMALAYA, GANGA, THE LETTER A.` · `VIBHUTI: WHERE GOD SHINES THROUGH.` · `THE BEST OF EACH KIND.` · `A HIDES INSIDE EVERY CONSONANT.` · then, large: `THE PLAINEST SOUND RUNS THROUGH ALL.`

segments.voice: Let the jaw soften, breathe in through the nose, and on the out-breath let a quiet, unshaped sound come out: a, like the start of the word about. Let it last as long as the breath, then rest in the silence. If you pray, let each a be a small bow to the one Krishna says runs through it; if not, just notice where the sound seems to come from. If sound isn't possible where you are, say it inwardly.
A. The open mouth, the plainest sound, the letter Krishna names among his shinings, hidden inside almost every letter on the page.
screen: `A — today's word`.

1041.title: Valmiki and the name said backwards
1041.hook: a robber can't bring himself to say Rama's name, so seven sages teach it to him backwards
1041.carry: nama japa: the name works, even said backwards
1041.tomorrow: what came out of Shiva's drum?
1041.howItsDone: Many Hindus practice nama japa, repeating a name of God aloud, silently, or in writing (likhita japa, filling notebooks with 'Shri Rama'); the story of Valmiki the robber, changed by repeating the name, is told to show that anyone may begin. Reciters also keep the long and short vowels of the name, as in Rāma.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-FORTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, vibhuti: Krishna shining in the best of everything, even the letter a. Today, a name built on that sound, and a robber who learned it backwards.
screen: `SACRED SOUNDS.` · `VIBHUTI: GOD SHINES THROUGH.`

segments.voice: Before he wrote the Ramayana, Valmiki was a robber. That's how he tells it himself, in a later Sanskrit retelling called the Adhyatma Ramayana. He lived among hunters and robbed travelers on the forest road. One day seven sages came down that road, and he raised his weapon. The sages didn't run. They asked him one question. Your family eats what you steal. Will they share the weight of what you've done? Go and ask them.
screen: `A ROBBER ON THE FOREST ROAD.` → `SEVEN SAGES.` → `WILL YOUR FAMILY SHARE IT?`

segments.voice: He went home and asked. Every one of them said no: that's yours. He came back shaken and fell at the sages' feet. They gave him the name of Rama to repeat, but in the telling they gave it to him backwards: mara. The way the story is usually explained, he was too far gone even to say it straight. Say mara, mara, mara, over and over, and listen. It turns into Rama, Rama. He sat and repeated it so long that an anthill, a valmika, rose up over his body. When the sages came back and called him out of it, he had a new name, for the anthill: Valmiki. Here's the teaching. It's called nama japa, repeating the name of God, and many Hindus hold it as the simplest practice there is, and one of the strongest. The robber didn't have to be good first. He didn't even have to say it right. The name did its work anyway. That's why some devotees fill whole notebooks writing Shri Rama, a practice called likhita japa, written japa, and why the name is said at the start of a journey and at the end of a life. Now listen to the name itself. Written carefully, Rāma has a small line over the first a. That line marks length, matra, the measure of a sound in time. A short vowel takes one measure; a long one about two. Rāma is long, then short: Raah-muh. Chanted again and again, that long ā is where the voice rests.

1042.title: Shiva's drum and the sacred sounds
1042.hook: at the end of Shiva's dance his drum sounds fourteen times, and a grammarian hears the alphabet
1042.carry: the sound itself is sacred: shiva's drum
1042.tomorrow: why was baby Krishna named in secret?
1042.howItsDone: Hindus treat sacred sound with care: the Vedas were passed mouth to ear for centuries, mantras are learned from a teacher syllable by syllable, and students recite the consonants row by row from the throat to the lips; tradition says the fourteen Shiva Sutras that open Panini's grammar sounded from Nataraja's drum.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-FORTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, nama japa: a robber changed by Rama's name, even said backwards, and matra, the long ā where the voice rests. Today, the other side of it: why the sounds themselves matter.
screen: `SACRED SOUNDS.` · `THE NAME WORKS, EVEN BACKWARDS.`

segments.voice: Picture Shiva as Nataraja, the dancer, ringed in flame. In one of his upper hands is a small drum shaped like an hourglass, the damaru. Grammarians tell a story about it. At the end of his dance, Shiva struck the drum fourteen times. And Panini, the great grammarian of Sanskrit, heard in those fourteen beats fourteen short lines of sounds, and made them the key to his whole grammar.
screen: `NATARAJA'S DRUM.` → `FOURTEEN BEATS.` → `PANINI HEARS THE SOUNDS.`

segments.voice: Those fourteen lines are still called the Shiva Sutras, and they open Panini's grammar. Whatever you make of the story, the teaching inside it is very Hindu: sound is sacred. In Nataraja's hand, the drum is commonly read as creation, the first sound from which the world unfolds, with the fire in another hand as its ending. The Vedas are called shruti, what was heard. For many centuries they were passed mouth to ear, teacher to student, and reciters guarded every sound so carefully that the chants came down remarkably intact. That's why a grandmother corrects a syllable. Not because God can't understand you, but because the sound is part of the offering. And it's why the alphabet is laid out like a map of the mouth. The first row of consonants is made at the back, in the throat: ka, kha, ga, gha, nga. The next at the palate: cha, chha, ja, jha, nya. Then a row at the roof of the mouth, for tomorrow. Then the teeth: ta, tha, da, dha, na. Last, the lips: pa, pha, ba, bha, ma. Say ka, cha, ta, pa, and the sound walks forward out of you. The map even solves a puzzle on the page: in careful spelling, c is always said ch. Cakra is chakra. Candra, the moon, is chandra. Yesterday said the name works even said wrong. Today adds the other half: saying it with care is a way of loving it.
screen: `THE SHIVA SUTRAS.` · `SHRUTI: WHAT WAS HEARD.` · `THE SOUND IS PART OF THE OFFERING.` · `THROAT, PALATE, ROOF, TEETH, LIPS.` · then, large: `CARE IS A WAY OF LOVING IT.`

segments.voice: One out-breath at a time, say slowly: ka, at the back of the throat; cha, the middle of the tongue rising; ta, at the teeth; pa, at the lips. Rest a breath, then walk the sounds forward again. If you pray, end with a mantra you know, each sound placed with care; if not, end with ma and let it fade into the breath.
Ka. The first consonant, made in the throat, where the map of the mouth begins: throat, palate, roof, teeth, lips.

1043.title: Krishna's secret naming
1043.hook: a sage names a baby in a cowshed, in secret, and calls him the dark one: Kṛṣṇa
1043.carry: namakarana: a name is a family's first blessing
1043.tomorrow: which letters carry an extra breath?
1043.howItsDone: Hindu families mark a baby's naming with namakarana, one of the samskaras: often in the first weeks, a priest is called, the name is whispered in the baby's right ear, and many take the first syllable from the birth star. Students of Sanskrit learn the retroflex sounds and the vowel ṛ in names like Kṛṣṇa.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-FORTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shiva's drum: the sound itself is sacred, and the map of the mouth. One row was skipped, the roof of the mouth. Today it gets its turn, inside a name.
screen: `SACRED SOUNDS.` · `THE SOUND ITSELF IS SACRED.`

segments.voice: In Gokula, among the cowherds, a baby is growing up who isn't safe. King Kamsa wants him dead. Then Garga, the family priest of the Yadus, arrives at the house of Nanda, the boy's foster father. Nanda asks him to perform the naming. Garga hesitates. If word gets out, Kamsa will guess who this child really is. So Nanda says: do it quietly, in the cowshed. No one will know.
screen: `A BABY WHO ISN'T SAFE.` → `A SAGE AT THE DOOR.` → `NAME HIM IN THE COWSHED.`

segments.voice: So in the cowshed, Garga names two boys. The older he calls Rama, for the joy he gives, and Bala, for his strength: Balarama. Then he looks at the dark little one. In the Bhagavata Purana he says, in paraphrase: in other ages this child came white, red and yellow. Now he has come dark. Kṛṣṇa. The name means dark, like a rain cloud. The ceremony is real, and Hindu families still do it. It's called namakarana, the naming, one of the samskaras, the rites that mark a life. Often in the first weeks, a priest is called, the name is whispered in the baby's right ear, and the family gives its first blessing. Many ask which star the baby was born under, since each birth star has starting sounds for a name. In this tradition a name isn't a label. It's a blessing said again every time someone calls you. Now read the name the careful way: K, r with a dot under it, s with a dot, n with a dot, a. Kṛṣṇa. Those dots belong to the roof of the mouth. Curl the tongue back and say ṭa, then ṇa: deeper, almost hollow. The s with a dot is a curled-back sh, as in Viṣṇu. And the r with a dot is a vowel of its own, ṛ. Some reciters say it close to ri, which gives us the spelling Krishna; others say it closer to ru. And the week: a palm that says do not fear, a dance offered, work as worship, a name repeated, a sound kept with care, and now a name given.
screen: `IN OTHER AGES, OTHER COLORS.` · `NOW HE HAS COME DARK: KṚṢṆA.` · `A NAME ISN'T A LABEL.` · `THE DOTS: THE TONGUE CURLS BACK.` · then, large: `A NAME IS A BLESSING.`

segments.voice: Say ta at the teeth, then curl the tongue back and say ṭa at the roof, back and forth a few times; then na and ṇa the same way. Then say the name slowly, piece by piece: kṛ, ṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa. If you pray, say it as a name, not a word. If not, say your own name slowly, and think of the first people who said it over you.
Ṛ. The r that is a vowel, at the heart of Kṛṣṇa, the name a sage gave in secret, in a cowshed.
